title: Good Leaders Don’t Allow Meeting Spectators
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article claims that nearly every team has members who sit silently in meetings, and that teams usually excuse this as personality rather than disengagement. The author argues that silence costs the team the wisdom and disagreement of those people and weakens decision quality. Good leaders refuse to let anyone remain a spectator and use a form of the Socratic method, asking everyone for views, opinions and knowledge. Setting an expectation that all come prepared and may be called on at random makes the conversation more robust. The result is a team benefiting from perspectives that would otherwise have been withheld. The closing line holds that meetings are never spectator sports.
points: Silent participants are usually excused as having a quiet personality, which hides the cost to the team.
Discussions missing the full range of voices are incomplete and degrade decision-making.
Socratic-style questioning directed at everyone, especially habitual spectators, keeps the room engaged.
Calling on people at random and expecting preparation makes active participation the norm.
quotes: The cast of characters typically remains the same. It is usually the same team members who watch the action in meetings and rarely, if ever, contribute to the discussion. They prefer to stay in the background and under the radar.

In most teams, their silence is accepted and viewed as a reflection of personality, not engagement. Whatever the underlying reason for their reticence, these team members are spectators and not full participants in team discussions.

Unfortunately, the team doesn’t benefit from their wisdom, disagreement, or point of view. Discussions without the full chorus of voices and viewpoints are incomplete. The quality of decision-making suffers as a result.

Good leaders don’t allow anyone to become a meeting or discussion spectator. Using a version of the Socratic method, the best leaders keep everyone engaged and on their toes by peppering them with questions.

When leaders ask everyone to come prepared for the discussion and to prove it by being capable and ready to answer any question on the topic under review, the conversation becomes much more robust. By calling on people randomly to respond or offer their view, the entire team becomes engaged and motivated to contribute.

Once an expectation is set that no one can sit passively or remain silent during team meetings, the group benefits from different perspectives and viewpoints that otherwise would have been withheld. Asking everyone to contribute, share their ideas, and become fully involved in the discussion is what good leaders do through their Socratic questioning. There is nothing more provocative than full engagement in a conversation.
